title: Overview — Gallbladder & Murphy's sign
model_answer:
## Gallbladder & Murphy's Sign – Complete Surgical OSCE Answer (Examination, Technique, Clinical Findings & Radiology)

### Topic importance

⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ Particularly important surgical examination topic. Covered as if standing in front of the examiner, including practical details they might challenge you on.

:::definition Definition
Murphy's sign is a clinical sign of acute cholecystitis, characterized by sudden cessation of inspiration due to pain when the examiner palpates the right upper quadrant over the gallbladder.
:::

### Sheet guide

- 1. Murphy's Technique (Q1)
- 2. Murphy Variations (Q2–Q6)
- 3. Other Signs (Q7–Q8)
- 4. Clinical Findings (Q9)
- 5. X-ray (Q10–Q11)
- 6. Examiner Q&A (Q12)
- 7. References (Q13)

:::pearl ⭐ 30-second answer to impress the examiner
Murphy's sign is a clinical sign of acute cholecystitis. I would position the patient supine, identify the right midclavicular line and costal margin, and place my right fingertips beneath the right costal margin over the gallbladder region. I would then ask the patient to take a deep breath. During inspiration, the diaphragm pushes the liver and gallbladder downwards against my fingers. If the gallbladder is inflamed, this produces significant pain, causing sudden arrest of inspiration. This constitutes a positive Murphy's sign.
:::

:::remember Three numbers/facts to remember
- 9th right costal cartilage.
- Approximately 15% of gallstones are visible on plain X-ray.
- Gallbladder wall thickness >3 mm on ultrasound is abnormal.
:::

### Good luck

Good luck with this station! 🌟
source: Dr. Salah — Gallbladder & Murphy's Sign OSCE workbook

title: Q1. How do you perform Murphy's sign?
model_answer:
:::definition Definition
Murphy's sign is a clinical sign of acute cholecystitis, characterized by sudden cessation of inspiration due to pain when the examiner palpates the right upper quadrant over the gallbladder.
:::

:::step 1 Preparation
- Introduce yourself.
- Confirm the patient's identity.
- Explain the procedure and obtain consent.
- Ask whether the patient has any abdominal pain.
- Position the patient supine.
- Expose the abdomen appropriately while maintaining privacy. You only need to expose the right upper quadrant.
:::

:::step 2 Locate the gallbladder
The gallbladder is located:
- In the right hypochondrium.
- Beneath the liver.
- Near the tip of the right 9th costal cartilage.
- At approximately the intersection of the right midclavicular line and the costal margin.

This is approximately the gallbladder's surface marking.
:::

:::step 3 Hand positioning
- Use your right hand (assuming you are right-handed).
- Place the fingertips of your right hand beneath the right costal margin.
- Position them over the gallbladder region, approximately at the lateral border of the right rectus abdominis muscle.
- Apply gentle but firm pressure.
:::

![Palpating beneath the right costal margin over the gallbladder: the examining fingers hook under the rib edge while the patient breathes in.](/clinical/murphy-palpation.jpg)

:::step 4 Ask the patient to breathe
Ask the patient: "Please take a slow, deep breath in."

During inspiration:
- The diaphragm descends.
- The liver and gallbladder move downwards.
- The inflamed gallbladder comes into contact with your examining fingers.
- This produces pain.
:::

:::step 5 Observe the patient's response
A positive Murphy's sign occurs when:
- The patient experiences significant pain.
- Inspiration is suddenly interrupted or arrested because of the pain.

This is called inspiratory arrest.

A positive Murphy's sign suggests acute cholecystitis.
:::

:::reference Reference
Murphy's Sign – Medical Journal of Australia
:::
source: Dr. Salah — Gallbladder & Murphy's Sign OSCE workbook

title: Q2. Perform Murphy's sign without exposing the patient
model_answer:
:::group
Q2–Q6. Murphy's Sign: Variations, Finger Placement, Hand, Instruction & Positive Result
:::

### Overview

This is an important practical OSCE variation. The examiner may ask you to demonstrate the technique while maintaining the patient's privacy.

![Examining the right upper quadrant with the abdomen kept covered by a sheet.](/clinical/murphy-through-sheet.png)

### What to do

1. Keep the patient covered with a sheet.
2. Identify the approximate location of the right costal margin through the sheet.
3. Place your fingertips over the right upper quadrant.
4. Apply gentle pressure through the sheet.
5. Ask the patient to take a deep breath.
6. Observe for inspiratory arrest due to pain.

:::say What to tell the examiner
"I would maintain the patient's dignity by keeping the abdomen covered and exposing only the necessary examination area. I would perform the maneuver over the right upper quadrant, ensuring that the patient is comfortable."
:::

:::important Important
The sheet should not interfere with proper palpation. If necessary, explain that you would expose only the examination site with the patient's consent.
:::
source: Dr. Salah — Gallbladder & Murphy's Sign OSCE workbook

title: Q3. Where exactly do you place your fingers?
model_answer:
:::group
Q2–Q6. Murphy's Sign: Variations, Finger Placement, Hand, Instruction & Positive Result
:::

### Anatomical precision

The classical anatomical location is: the intersection of the right midclavicular line and the right costal margin, near the tip of the ninth costal cartilage.

### More practically

- Right upper quadrant.
- Just below the right costal margin.
- Near the lateral border of the right rectus abdominis.

Your fingers should be positioned to palpate the gallbladder as it descends during inspiration.

:::important Important distinction
Murphy's sign is not simply pressing over the liver. You are specifically trying to elicit tenderness over the gallbladder.
:::
source: Dr. Salah — Gallbladder & Murphy's Sign OSCE workbook

title: Q4. Which hand do you use?
model_answer:
:::group
Q2–Q6. Murphy's Sign: Variations, Finger Placement, Hand, Instruction & Positive Result
:::

### Hand

Use your right hand if you are right-handed. The right hand performs the palpation. The left hand can be used for support or stabilization if necessary.

The classical technique involves placing the examining fingers beneath the right costal margin.

### Seated variation

The examiner may also ask you to demonstrate the technique with the patient sitting. The original description involved examining the patient from behind while the patient was seated.

Modern clinical examinations commonly perform it with the patient supine.

:::reference Reference
Radiographics – Improving Diagnosis of Acute Cholecystitis with US
:::
source: Dr. Salah — Gallbladder & Murphy's Sign OSCE workbook

title: Q5. What do you ask the patient to do?
model_answer:
:::group
Q2–Q6. Murphy's Sign: Variations, Finger Placement, Hand, Instruction & Positive Result
:::

### Instruction

Ask: "Please take a slow, deep breath in."

Do not ask the patient to breathe out.

### Why? (physiological basis)

During inspiration:
1. The diaphragm contracts and descends.
2. The liver moves downwards.
3. The gallbladder descends.
4. The inflamed gallbladder contacts your examining fingers.
5. Pain causes sudden inspiratory arrest.
source: Dr. Salah — Gallbladder & Murphy's Sign OSCE workbook

title: Q6. What makes Murphy's sign positive?
model_answer:
:::group
Q2–Q6. Murphy's Sign: Variations, Finger Placement, Hand, Instruction & Positive Result
:::

:::definition Definition
Sudden cessation of inspiration due to pain when the examiner palpates the right upper quadrant during deep inspiration.

The patient cannot complete the inspiratory effort because of severe tenderness.

It is classically associated with acute calculous cholecystitis.
:::

:::remember Remember
- Tenderness alone is not the classical definition.
- The characteristic feature is inspiratory arrest due to pain.
:::
source: Dr. Salah — Gallbladder & Murphy's Sign OSCE workbook

title: Q7. If Murphy's sign is positive, what other signs do you look for?
model_answer:
:::group
Q7–Q8. Other Signs if Murphy's Is Positive; Boas' Sign
:::

### Overview

You should look for additional evidence of acute cholecystitis.

### A. Local abdominal signs

1. Right hypochondrial tenderness.
2. Guarding over the right upper quadrant.
3. Rebound tenderness if peritoneal irritation is present.
4. Positive Murphy's sign.
5. Palpable tender gallbladder in some patients.

### B. Systemic signs

- Fever.
- Tachycardia.
- Tachypnea.
- Signs of systemic inflammation.

### C1. Boas' sign

Hyperesthesia or tenderness in the right infrascapular region (below the right scapula).

### C2. Courvoisier's sign/law

A palpable, enlarged, non-tender gallbladder associated with painless obstructive jaundice suggests malignant obstruction rather than gallstone disease.

Classically associated with carcinoma of the head of the pancreas.

### C3. Charcot's triad

Important if you suspect associated acute cholangitis:
- Fever.
- Right upper quadrant pain.
- Jaundice.

If hypotension and altered mental status are also present, this constitutes Reynolds' pentad.

:::tip OSCE tip
A patient with acute cholecystitis does not necessarily have jaundice. Significant or persistent jaundice should make you consider common bile duct obstruction or associated cholangitis.
:::

:::reference Reference
Current Medical Diagnosis & Treatment 2027 – Acute Cholecystitis
:::
source: Dr. Salah — Gallbladder & Murphy's Sign OSCE workbook

title: Q8. What is Boas' sign?
model_answer:
:::group
Q7–Q8. Other Signs if Murphy's Is Positive; Boas' Sign
:::

:::definition Definition
Boas' sign is an area of hyperesthesia or tenderness below the right scapula, associated with acute cholecystitis.
:::

![Boas' sign. A: the right infrascapular region. B: pointing to the area below the right scapula where hyperaesthesia or tenderness is sought.](/clinical/boas-sign.jpg)

### Why does it happen?

The gallbladder and surrounding structures share visceral sensory pathways. Inflammation of the gallbladder can produce referred pain and altered sensitivity in the right infrascapular region.

### How do you examine it?

1. Ask the patient to sit or stand.
2. Expose the back appropriately.
3. Examine the area below the right scapula.
4. Gently compare sensitivity with the corresponding area on the left side.
5. Look for increased tenderness or hyperesthesia on the right.

### Positive Boas' sign

Increased sensitivity or tenderness below the right scapula.

:::remember Remember
- Murphy's sign → Right upper quadrant.
- Boas' sign → Right infrascapular region.
:::
source: Dr. Salah — Gallbladder & Murphy's Sign OSCE workbook

title: Q9. What are the clinical findings of acute cholecystitis? (common long-case and viva question)
model_answer:
## A. History

### 1. Pain

- Acute onset.
- Severe, persistent pain.
- Located in the right hypochondrium or epigastrium.
- Often follows a fatty meal.
- May radiate to the right shoulder or right scapular region.
- Unlike uncomplicated biliary colic, the pain persists rather than resolving spontaneously within a few hours.

### 2. Associated symptoms

- Nausea.
- Vomiting.
- Fever.
- Anorexia.
- Occasionally jaundice.

## B. Physical examination

| Finding | Details |
|---|---|
| Fever | Usually present |
| Right hypochondrial tenderness | Common |
| Murphy's sign | Often positive |
| Guarding | May be present |
| Rebound tenderness | May occur with peritoneal irritation |
| Tachycardia | May be present |
| Palpable gallbladder | Occasionally present |
| Jaundice | May occur, but consider CBD obstruction |

## C. Investigations

### 1. Blood – CBC

- Leukocytosis.
- Neutrophilia.

### Blood – CRP

Elevated.

### Blood – Liver function tests

- Mild elevations in AST and ALT.
- ALP and bilirubin may be elevated.

Significant abnormalities should raise suspicion of common bile duct stones or associated cholangitis.

### Blood – Amylase/lipase

May be elevated if associated with gallstone pancreatitis.

### 2. Ultrasound abdomen

This is the first-line imaging investigation.

Findings include:
1. Gallstones.
2. Gallbladder wall thickening (usually >3 mm).
3. Gallbladder distension.
4. Pericholecystic fluid.
5. Sonographic Murphy's sign.

### Sonographic Murphy's sign

Maximum tenderness when the ultrasound probe is placed directly over the gallbladder.

Do not confuse this with clinical Murphy's sign.
source: Dr. Salah — Gallbladder & Murphy's Sign OSCE workbook

title: Q10. X-ray findings in acute cholecystitis
model_answer:
:::group
Q10–Q11. X-ray Findings in Acute Cholecystitis; Visibility of Gallstones
:::

Examiners sometimes ask about the plain abdominal X-ray. Plain abdominal X-ray is NOT the investigation of choice for acute cholecystitis. However, it may demonstrate:

### 1. Radiopaque gallstones

Gallstones containing sufficient calcium may be visible on plain abdominal radiographs.

### 2. Porcelain gallbladder

Calcification of the gallbladder wall. It appears as curvilinear or circumferential calcification in the right upper quadrant.

### 3. Emphysematous cholecystitis

Gas within:
- The gallbladder wall.
- The gallbladder lumen.
- Occasionally the surrounding tissues.

:::note Note
Associated with gas-forming organisms and is a potentially life-threatening complication.
:::

### 4. Other findings

- Localized ileus.
- Occasionally a nonspecific soft-tissue shadow.
- Rarely, pneumobilia or features of gallstone ileus when associated complications are present.

:::important Important
Plain radiographs are not sufficiently sensitive or specific to diagnose acute cholecystitis.
:::

:::reference Reference
Reference: Japanese Guidelines for Diagnostic Imaging 2021 – Plain Radiography
:::
source: Dr. Salah — Gallbladder & Murphy's Sign OSCE workbook

title: Q11. What percentage of gallstones are visible on plain X-ray?
model_answer:
:::group
Q10–Q11. X-ray Findings in Acute Cholecystitis; Visibility of Gallstones
:::

:::pearl Answer
⭐ Approximately 10–15%. A commonly quoted textbook figure is 15%.
:::

:::say Exam answer
15% of gallstones are visible on plain abdominal X-ray.
:::

### Why?

Most gallstones are cholesterol-rich and are radiolucent. Only stones containing sufficient calcium are radiopaque and visible on plain X-ray.

:::reference Reference
Source: Current Medical Diagnosis & Treatment 2027.
:::

| Types of gallstones and radiological visibility | Composition | Plain X-ray |
|---|---|---|
| Cholesterol stones | Mainly cholesterol | Usually radiolucent |
| Black pigment stones | Calcium bilirubinate and other calcium salts | Sometimes radiopaque |
| Brown pigment stones | Calcium bilirubinate and other components | Usually radiolucent or poorly visible |
| Mixed stones | Cholesterol, calcium salts and other components | Variable |
source: Dr. Salah — Gallbladder & Murphy's Sign OSCE workbook
